listen_text: Section. Introduction. In the source passage on chap , we postulated that there is an infinite-th stage of the hierarchy, in the form of Stages hit infinity (see also our axiom of Infinity). However, given Stages keep going, we can't stop at the infinite-th stage; we have to keep going. So: at the next stage after the first infinite stage, we form all possible collections of sets that were available at the first infinite stage; and repeat; and repeat; and repeat; and so on Implicitly what has happened here is that we have started to invoke an “intuitive” notion of number, according to which there can be numbers after all the natural numbers. In particular, the notion involved is that of a transfinite ordinal. The aim of this chapter is to make this idea more rigorous. We will explore the general notion of an ordinal, and then explicitly define certain sets to be our ordinals. End section.

Section. The General Idea of an Ordinal. Consider the natural numbers, in their usual order: The diagram expands a source loop. In that loop, the current loop value successively takes the values zero through five. Each displayed value is less than the next. After five the diagram continues, and so on . Thus, from left to right: zero is less than one, one is less than two, two is less than three, three is less than four, four is less than five, and the sequence continues. End diagram. We call this, in the jargon, an omega -sequence. And indeed, this general ordering is mirrored in our initial construction of the stages of the set hierarchy. But, now suppose we move zero to the end of this sequence, so that it comes after all the other numbers: In the source loop, the current loop value successively takes the values one through five. Each loop value is ordered before the next. After five the positive-number sequence continues, and so on . The entire continuing sequence is ordered before the final zero . The resulting order has all positive natural numbers first and zero last. End diagram. We have the same entities here, but ordered in a fundamentally different way: our first ordering had no last element; our new ordering does. Indeed, our new ordering consists of an omega -sequence of entities ( one, then two, then three, then four, then five, and so on ), followed by another entity. It will be an omega plus one -sequence. We can generate even more types of ordering, using just these entities. For example, consider all the even numbers (in their natural order) followed by all the odd numbers (in their natural order): The diagram reads left to right. The first displayed value is zero ; it is ordered before two , which is ordered before four . Four is ordered before the later even natural numbers, and so on . The entire continuing even sequence is ordered before one , which is ordered before three . Three is ordered before the later odd natural numbers, and so on . It places every even natural number in increasing order before every odd natural number in increasing order. End diagram. This is an omega -sequence followed by another omega -sequence; an omega plus omega -sequence. Well, we can keep going. But what we would like is a general way to understand this talk about orderings. End section.

listen_text: Section. Von Neumann's Construction of the Ordinals. the theorem on woalwayscomparable gives rise to a thought. We could introduce certain objects, called order types, to go proxy for the well-orderings. Writing the order type of capital A under the less-than relation for the order type of the well-ordering the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation , we would hope to secure the following two principles: Displayed expression. Two proposed order-type principles. First, the order type of capital A under less-than equals the order type of capital B under less-dot if and only if those two well-orderings are order-isomorphic. Second, the first order type is less than the second if and only if the first well-ordering is order-isomorphic to the initial segment of capital B below some b. End principles. End displayed expression. Moreover, we might hope to introduce order-types as certain sets, just as we can introduce the natural numbers as certain sets. The most common way to do this—and the approach we will follow—is to define these order-types via certain canonical well-ordered sets. These canonical sets were first introduced by von Neumann: Definition. The set capital A is transitive if and only if for every x in capital A, x is a subset of capital A . Then capital A is an ordinal if and only if capital A is transitive and well-ordered by the membership relation . End definition. In what follows, we will use Greek letters for ordinals. It follows immediately from the definition that, if alpha is an ordinal, then the ordered pair consisting of alpha and membership restricted to alpha is a well-ordering, where membership restricted to alpha equals the set of ordered pairs x and y in alpha squared such that x belongs to y . So, abusing notation a little, we can just say that alpha itself is a well-ordering. Here are our first few ordinals: Displayed expression. the empty set; then the singleton containing the empty set; then the set containing the empty set and that singleton; then the set containing the empty set, that singleton, and the preceding two-element set; and so on. End displayed expression. You will note that these are the first few ordinals that we encountered in our Axiom of Infinity, that is, in von Neumann's definition of omega (see the source passage on sec ). This is no coincidence. Von Neumann's definition of the ordinals treats natural numbers as ordinals, but allows for transfinite ordinals too. As always, we can now ask: are these the ordinals? Or has von Neumann simply given us some sets that we can treat as the ordinals? The kinds of discussions one might have about this question are similar to the discussions we had in the source passage on sec , the source passage on sec , the source passage on sec , and the source passage on sec , so we will not belabour the point. Instead, in what follows, we will simply use “the ordinals” to speak of “the von Neumann ordinals”. End section.

listen_text: Section. Basic Properties of the Ordinals. We observed that the first few ordinals are the natural numbers. The main reason for developing a theory of ordinals is to extend the principle of induction which holds on the natural numbers. We will build up to this via a sequence of elementary results. Lemma. Every element of an ordinal is an ordinal. End lemma. Proof. Let alpha be an ordinal with b belongs to alpha . Since alpha is transitive, b is a subset of alpha . So the membership relation well-orders b as the membership relation well-orders alpha . To see that b is transitive, suppose x belongs to c, and c belongs to b . So c belongs to alpha as b is a subset of alpha . Again, as alpha is transitive, c is a subset of alpha , so that x belongs to alpha . So x, c, and b belong to alpha . But the membership relation well-orders alpha , so that the membership relation is a transitive relation on alpha by the source passage on strictorder . So since x belongs to c, and c belongs to b , we have x belongs to b . Generalising, c is a subset of b End proof. Corollary. alpha equals the set of ordinals beta that belong to alpha , for any ordinal alpha End corollary. Proof. Immediate from the source passage on ordmemberord . End proof. The rough gist of the next two main results, the source passage on ordinductionschema and the source passage on ordtrichotomy , is that the ordinals themselves are well-ordered by membership: Theorem. Transfinite Induction. For any formula phi of x : Displayed expression. if some alpha satisfies phi, then there is an alpha satisfying phi such that no beta belonging to alpha satisfies phi. End displayed expression. where the displayed quantifiers are implicitly restricted to ordinals. End theorem. Proof. Suppose phi of alpha , for some ordinal alpha . If for every beta in alpha, not phi of beta , then we are done. Otherwise, as alpha is an ordinal, it has some the membership relation -least element which is phi , and this is an ordinal by the source passage on ordmemberord . End proof. Note that we can equally express the source passage on ordinductionschema as the scheme: Displayed expression. if phi holds of every alpha whenever it holds of every beta belonging to alpha, then phi holds of every alpha. End displayed expression. just by taking not phi of alpha in the source passage on ordinductionschema , and then performing elementary logical manipulations. Theorem. Trichotomy. alpha belongs to beta or alpha equals beta or beta belongs to alpha , for any ordinals alpha and beta . End theorem. Proof. The proof is by double induction, that is, using the source passage on ordinductionschema twice. Say that x is comparable with y if and only if x belongs to y or x equals y or y belongs to x . For induction, suppose that every ordinal in alpha is comparable with every ordinal. For further induction, suppose that alpha is comparable with every ordinal in beta . We will show that alpha is comparable with beta . By induction on beta , it will follow that alpha is comparable with every ordinal; and so by induction on alpha , every ordinal is comparable with every ordinal, as required. It suffices to assume that alpha does not belong to beta and beta does not belong to alpha , and show that alpha equals beta . To show that alpha is a subset of beta , fix gamma belongs to alpha ; this is an ordinal by the source passage on ordmemberord . So by the first induction hypothesis, gamma is comparable with beta . But if either gamma equals beta or beta belongs to gamma then beta belongs to alpha (invoking the fact that alpha is transitive if necessary), contrary to our assumption; so gamma belongs to beta . Generalising, alpha is a subset of beta . Exactly similar reasoning, using the second induction hypothesis, shows that beta is a subset of alpha . So alpha equals beta . End proof. As such, we will sometimes write alpha is less than beta rather than alpha belongs to beta , since the membership relation is behaving as an ordering relation. There are no deep reasons for this, beyond familiarity, and because it is easier to write alpha is less than or equal to beta than alpha belongs to beta or alpha equals beta . Footnote. We could write alpha bears the underlined membership relation to beta ; but that would be wholly non-standard. End footnote. Here are two quick consequences of our last results, the first of which puts our new notation into action: Corollary. If there exists alpha, phi of alpha , then there exists an alpha satisfying phi such that every beta satisfying phi is greater than or equal to alpha . Moreover, for any ordinals alpha, then beta, then gamma , both alpha does not belong to alpha and if alpha belongs to beta and beta belongs to gamma, then alpha belongs to gamma . End corollary. Proof. Just like the source passage on strictorder . End proof. Exercise. Complete the “exactly similar reasoning” in the proof of the source passage on ordtrichotomy . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Corollary. capital A is an ordinal if and only if capital A is a transitive set of ordinals. End corollary. Proof. Left-to-right. By the source passage on ordmemberord . Right-to-left. If capital A is a transitive set of ordinals, then the membership relation well-orders capital A by the source passage on ordinductionschema and the source passage on ordtrichotomy . End proof. Now, we glossed the source passage on ordinductionschema and the source passage on ordtrichotomy as telling us that the membership relation well-orders the ordinals. However, we have to be very cautious about this sort of claim, thanks to the following result: Theorem. Burali-Forti Paradox. There is no set of all the ordinals End theorem. Proof. For reductio, suppose capital O is the set of all ordinals. If alpha belongs to beta, and beta belongs to capital O , then alpha is an ordinal, by the source passage on ordmemberord , so alpha belongs to capital O . So capital O is transitive, and hence capital O is an ordinal by the source passage on corordtransitiveord . Hence capital O belongs to capital O , contradicting the source passage on ordordered . End proof. This result is named after the cited work Burali- Fortioneeightnineseven . But, it was Cantor in one thousand eight hundred ninety nine—in a letter to Dedekind—who first saw clearly the contradiction in supposing that there is a set of all the ordinals. As van Heijenoort explains: Quotation. Burali-Forti himself considered the contradiction as establishing, by reductio ad absurdum, the result that the natural ordering of the ordinals is just a partial ordering. the cited work by Heijenoort from nineteen hundred sixty seven End quotation. Setting Burali-Forti's mistake to one side, we can summarize the foregoing as follows. Ordinals are sets which are individually well-ordered by membership, and collectively well-ordered by membership (without collectively constituting a set). listen_text: Section. Replacement. In the source passage on sec , we motivated the introduction of ordinals by suggesting that we could treat them as order-types, that is, canonical proxies for well-orderings. In order for that to work, we would need to prove that every well-ordering is isomorphic to some ordinal. This would allow us to define the order type of capital A under the less-than relation as the ordinal alpha such that capital A under less-than is isomorphic to alpha . Unfortunately, we cannot prove the desired result only the Axioms we provided introduced so far. (We will see why in the source passage on sec , but for now the point is: we can't.) We need a new thought, and here it is: Axiom. Scheme of Replacement. For any formula phi of x and y , the following is an axiom: Quotation. for any capital A , if for every x in capital A, there exists exactly one y, phi of x and y , then the set of y such that there exists x in capital A, phi of x and y exists. End quotation. End axiom. As with Separation, this is a scheme: it yields infinitely many axioms, for each of the infinitely many different phi apostrophe s . And it can equally well be (and normally is) written down thus: For any formula phi of x and y which does not contain “ capital B ”, the following is an axiom: Displayed expression. for every capital A, if every x in capital A has exactly one y such that phi holds of x and y, then there exists a capital B such that, for every y, y belongs to capital B if and only if phi holds of x and y for some x in capital A. End displayed expression. On first encounter, however, this is quite a tangled formula. The following quick consequence of Replacement probably gives a clearer expression to the intuitive idea we are working with: Footnote. A term is an expression which picks out exactly one object (on any completion of its free variables). For example, “ the empty set ” is a term which picks out the empty set; “ the set containing x ” is a term which picks out x apostrophe s singleton (whatever x might be); “ x union y ” is a term which picks out the union of x and y (whatever they might be). End footnote. Corollary. For any term tau of x , and any set capital A , this set exists: Displayed expression. the set of tau of x such that x belongs to capital A, equals the set of y such that there exists x in capital A, y equals tau of x. End displayed expression. End corollary. Proof. Since tau is a term, for every x, there exists exactly one y, tau of x equals y . A fortiori, for every x in capital A, there exists exactly one y, tau of x equals y . So the set of y such that there exists x in capital A, tau of x equals y exists by Replacement. End proof. This suggests that “Replacement” is a good name for the Axiom: given a set capital A , you can form a new set, the set of tau of x such that x belongs to capital A , by replacing every member of capital A with its image under tau . Indeed, following the notation for the image of a set under a function, we might write the image of capital A under tau for the set of tau of x such that x belongs to capital A . Crucially, however, tau is a term. It need not be (a name for) a function, in the sense of the source passage on sec , that is, a certain set of ordered pairs. After all, if f is a function (in that sense), then the set the image of capital A under f equals the set of f of x such that x belongs to capital A is just a particular subset of the range of f , and that is already guaranteed to exist, just using the axioms of set theory Z minus . Footnote. Just consider the set of y in the double union of f such that y equals f of x for some x in capital A . End footnote. Replacement, by contrast, is a powerful addition to our axioms, as we will see in the source passage on chap . End section.

listen_text: Section. set theory Z F minus : a milestone. The question of how to justify Replacement (if at all) is not straightforward. As such, we will reserve that for the source passage on chap . However, with the addition of Replacement, we have reached another important milestone. We now have all the axioms required for the theory set theory Z F minus . In detail: Definition. The theory set theory Z F minus has these axioms: Extensionality, Union, Pairs, Powersets, Infinity, and all instances of the Separation and Replacement schemes. Otherwise put, set theory Z F minus adds Replacement to set theory Z minus . End definition. This stands for Zermelo—Fraenkel set theory ( minus something which we will come to later). Fraenkel gets the honour, since he is credited with the formulation of Replacement in the cited work by Fraenkel from nineteen hundred twenty two , although the first precise formulation was due to the cited work by Skolem from nineteen hundred twenty two . End section.

Every well-ordering is isomorphic to a unique ordinal. End theorem. Proof. Let the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation be a well-order. By the source passage on ordisoidentity , it is isomorphic to at most one ordinal. So, for reductio, suppose the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation is not isomorphic to any ordinal. We will first “make the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation as small as possible”. Otherwise, let capital B equals capital A and the less-dot relation equals the less-than relation . So by Replacement, the following set exists, and is a function: Displayed expression. f equals the set of ordered pairs beta and b such that b belongs to capital B and beta is order-isomorphic to the initial segment capital B subscript b under restricted less-dot. If the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation is a well-ordering, then its order type, the order type of capital A under the less-than relation , is the unique ordinal alpha such that capital A under less-than is order-isomorphic to alpha . End definition. Moreover, this definition licenses two nice principles: Corollary. listen_text: Section. Successor and Limit Ordinals. In the next few chapters, we will use ordinals a great deal. So it will help if we introduce some simple notions. Definition. For any ordinal alpha , its successor is the ordinal successor of alpha equals alpha union the set containing alpha . We say that alpha is a successor ordinal if the ordinal successor of beta equals alpha for some ordinal beta . We say that alpha is a limit ordinal if and only if alpha is neither empty nor a successor ordinal. End definition. The following result shows that this is the right notion of successor: Proposition. For any ordinal alpha : List. Next item. alpha belongs to the ordinal successor of alpha ; Next item. the ordinal successor of alpha is an ordinal; Next item. there is no ordinal beta such that alpha belongs to beta, and beta belongs to the ordinal successor of alpha . End list. End proposition. Proof. Trivially, alpha belongs to alpha union the set containing alpha equals the ordinal successor of alpha . Equally, the ordinal successor of alpha is a transitive set of ordinals, and hence an ordinal by the source passage on corordtransitiveord . And it is impossible that alpha belongs to beta, and beta belongs to the ordinal successor of alpha , since then either beta belongs to alpha or beta equals alpha , contradicting the source passage on ordordered . End proof. This also licenses a variant of proof by transfinite induction: Theorem. Simple Transfinite Induction. Let phi of x be a formula such that: List. Next item. phi of the empty set ; and Next item. for any ordinal alpha , if phi of alpha then phi of the ordinal successor of alpha ; and Next item. if alpha is a limit ordinal and for every beta in alpha, phi of beta , then phi of alpha . End list. Then for every alpha, phi of alpha . End theorem. Proof. We prove the contrapositive. So, suppose there is some ordinal which is not phi ; let gamma be the least such ordinal. Then either gamma equals the empty set , or gamma equals the ordinal successor of alpha for some alpha such that phi of alpha ; or gamma is a limit ordinal and for every beta in gamma, phi of beta . End proof. A final bit of notation will prove helpful later on: Definition. If capital X is a set of ordinals, then the strict supremum of capital X equals the union, over alpha in capital X, of the ordinal successors of alpha . End definition. Here, “lsub” stands for “least strict upper bound”. Footnote. Some books use “ the supremum of capital X ” for this. But other books use “ the supremum of capital X ” for the least non-strict upper bound, that is, simply the union of capital X . If capital X has a greatest element, alpha , these notions come apart: the least strict upper bound is the ordinal successor of alpha , whereas the least non-strict upper bound is just alpha . End footnote. The following result explains this: Proposition. If capital X is a set of ordinals, the strict supremum of capital X is the least ordinal greater than every ordinal in capital X . End proposition. Proof. Let capital Y equals the set of ordinal successors of alpha as alpha ranges over capital X , so that the strict supremum of capital X equals the union of capital Y . Since ordinals are transitive and every member of an ordinal is an ordinal, the strict supremum of capital X is a transitive set of ordinals, and so is an ordinal by the source passage on corordtransitiveord . If alpha belongs to capital X , then the ordinal successor of alpha belongs to capital Y , so the ordinal successor of alpha is a subset of the union of capital Y equals the strict supremum of capital X , and hence alpha belongs to the strict supremum of capital X . So the strict supremum of capital X is strictly greater than every ordinal in capital X . Conversely, if alpha belongs to the strict supremum of capital X , then alpha belongs to the ordinal successor of beta, and that successor belongs to capital Y for some beta belongs to capital X , so that alpha is less than or equal to beta, and beta belongs to capital X . So the strict supremum of capital X is the least strict upper bound on capital X . End proof. End section. End chapter.
